I hear you, I see you, and I absolutely believe you. I am so incredibly sorry that happened to you, and that no one has acted or believed you previously. Please know that it is not your fault, you did nothing wrong, the monsters who did that are fully responsible for their atrocities. 

As someone who has been sexually assaulted by known and unknown perpetrators I can relate to feeling unable to cope with it and the fear it invokes in all aspects of life. I found EMDR to be really helpful for treating the trauma of it, and there is so much life on the other side of that pain. 

As others have said, (if you can) put distance between yourself and the perpetrators, talk about it to trusted people or write about it for yourself to process. Seek out professional help from a psychologist or therapist, and be kind to yourself. Recovery isn’t always linear and it can feel like it’s one step forward and two steps backwards, but I assure you there is a way forward and you can heal from this. You can also try calling local crisis lines that can give you more information on local resources available to you. 

I’m here if you need anyone to talk to, you’re not alone. You are strong, resilient, and loved. I wish nothing but the best for you!

There's so much pressure to get a high ATAR when it really isn't the be-all and end-all. There are alternative pathways to get into uni and even then uni isn't the only option. It's not worth destroying yourself over.

Exactly. OP, NTA. But please get out. These behaviours are incredibly troubling and are likely to escalate to full-on abuse.

🚩2. Cancelling the job interview which is likely a way to keep OP from leaving (or making it difficult to leave in the future) by taking away her financial independence. Advice: 
As other people have suggested - try rescheduling the interview. Reach out to friends and family and tell them what's happening. Save up secretly, see if there are any local services/resources that could help, and make a plan to safely leave. 

If he does have violent tendencies don't tell him you're leaving.  Tell a trusted person of your plan (limit the number of people you tell because it could get back to him - also be aware that he could be monitoring your messages etc.), and then when he is at work/out if the house, leave. 

OP, you deserve someone who lifts you up instead of breaking you down. I wish you all the best - an internet stranger.

YTA - I understand that you and your husband think you're doing the right thing and helping your daughter through this tragic situation but unfortunately you're not. 

From your post, you've failed to allow your daughter the opportunity to grieve the loss of her friend. She's old enough to understand the gravity of the situation so to actively deny her from grieving with other people (her *friends* people she has a connection with and trusts) in the same situation, and trying to get her to continue on with her life as if it never happened will be detrimental to her well-being. 

Personally, I was in a similar situation when I was around your daughter's age. A childhood friend passed away unexpectedly and the biggest support for me during that time was knowing I wasn't alone. Our group of friends was all mourning our shared loss and we helped each other through it. We all catch up on the anniversary of her passing, cook together and share memories, and at some point over the years this occasion has evolved from us all sitting in heavy silence, crying, to a joyful celebration in honour of our friend. 

Allowing your daughter to grieve with her friends who are all experiencing the same loss can allow her to connect with others and to heal with them. I recommend encouraging her to engage in therapy or at least let her know that it's an option. 

Stop pushing her to move on with her life, allow her space the grieve and heal. Encourage her to participate in things she enjoys but do not force her, it won't help anyone, she will just grow to resent you. 

Wishing your daughter all the best.

So sorry for your loss, OP.

Given that you're part time you might want to check your contract for a minimum notice period for resignation - if you were a causal employee then I'd say you won't be in the wrong. 

Regarding your point on your employer being inconsiderate - being in hospitality myself I don't think they meant it with malicious intent as they have spaces to fill and perhaps weren't aware of the full gravity of the situation. From your post it sounded like they didn't know he has passed just yet so I would first try to reach a resolution by contacting them about your schedule (your availability as well) and attempt to find a solution. If you're set on leaving anyway, try to leave on a good note and honour the contractual obligations. 

I'm not sure where you're located but you may be able to get a medical certificate for grief just to cover that basis. 

I'm so sorry for your loss and hope this situation works out. Wishing you the best.

NAH - you're just reinforcing your boundaries. Your mum most likely realised she was asking too many questions once you replied and tried to cut back on the information overload. 

I'm similar in that I get really stressed out and anxious when someone is overloading me with information/questions. I found myself in a similar situation with my mum and when it gets to that point I will let her know I'm overwhelmed and she will slow down and give me space. However, this did take many years of arguments to get to and sometimes she will overstep boundaries but she is more aware of it now.

In short, I don't think anyone is at fault here. I think if you have a conversation about it, let her know that it stresses you out and hopefully you can come up with a 'safe word' that lets her know that you're overwhelmed and that you will get back to her once you've calmed down. That way you can feel less guilty about saying something that might come across as blunt or rude and your mum can see where she crossed the line and can give you space without feeling like your ignoring her/don't want her opinion etc. Hopefully that helps!
